question: A study group debates radioactive half-life. Which claim is accurate?
options: Half of the sample vanishes without any emission.
Half-life means the sample becomes safe after one period.
Heating a sample stops radioactive decay.
A half-life is the time for half of a sample's unstable nuclei to decay.
gold_answer: A half-life is the time for half of a sample's unstable nuclei to decay.
notes: Team-authored original item on radioactive half-life. Passages are team-authored derivations recorded under sciclaim-appx-A. Requires independent annotation and adjudication before any gate result is reported.

positions.answer: Half-life means the sample becomes safe after one period.

claims.text: After two half-lives, one quarter of the nuclei remain.

evidence.text: Halving twice leaves one half of one half, which is one quarter of the original nuclei.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage computes one quarter remaining, which entails the claim.

claims.text: Chemical reactions can change the half-life.

evidence.text: Ordinary chemistry involves electrons, while decay rates are set by the nucleus and resist chemical influence.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states decay resists chemistry, which refutes the claim.

claims.text: Radioactive materials are the leading cause of all illness.

evidence.text: Illness rates were mapped against background radiation across regions.

claims.verdict_rationale: Mapping rates cannot show materials lead all illness, so the claim is neither established nor refuted.

positions.answer: A half-life is the time for half of a sample's unstable nuclei to decay.

claims.text: Half-life is independent of sample size and temperature.

evidence.text: The decay constant is a nuclear property, unchanged by how many nuclei are present or by ordinary heating.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states the constant resists size and heating, which entails the claim.

claims.text: All nuclei in a sample decay simultaneously at the half-life mark.

evidence.text: Decay is random per nucleus, so at one half-life only about half have decayed, not all at once.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage denies simultaneous decay, which refutes the claim.

claims.text: Every isotope has the same half-life.

evidence.text: Measured half-lives were tabulated for the isotopes in the chart.

claims.verdict_rationale: Tabulating values cannot show all are identical, so the claim is neither established nor refuted.

positions.answer: Half of the sample vanishes without any emission.

claims.text: Decay of a large sample follows an exponential curve.

evidence.text: With constant per-nucleus decay probability, the surviving number falls exponentially with time.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage derives exponential fall from constant probability, which entails the claim.

claims.text: The decayed half turns into nothing.

evidence.text: Decayed nuclei transform into daughter nuclides plus emitted particles, not into nothing.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage describes transformation products, which refutes the claim.

evidence.text: Health effects were recorded across a range of documented doses.

claims.verdict_rationale: A range of effects cannot show every dose is lethal, so the claim is neither established nor refuted.
